Actually, does anybody know if it's been explained before? If not, does anybody care to explain it? Sure, it can be found in the PIE thread on FF: Diamonds often occur as an early sign of a reversal and the reason for it is to trap as much retail money as possible, it tends to trap buyers and sellers then resolves very quickly after it completes a cycle of trapping retail. A diamond represents caution above all else because there is no clear defined momentum either way. But from a price structure point of view, its difficult to hold any position, buy or sell for any period of time or profit. Why diamonds occur near reversals is that the market wants to take out all buyers and sellers and then resolve quickly and the shape of the diamond does that. Its a trend traders nightmare and a scalpers or range traders ideal situation. Check this box to be notified of replies to this topic. Note: BBcode and smileys are still usable. Report to moderator Quick Reply Reply Quote Thank You Pedini's trades and setups 23 Jun 2013 05:31 #241 Harry --> Offline Master Trader Posts: 941 Thank you received: 2903 Hotochin wrote: Hey Harry I have got a question for you. How do you know that is the FL? Sometimes you will get multiple RBR levels that could act as FL. Even in your chart, couldn't that level below make a FL? Thanks, H you are quite right there Hotochin, you see FLs (or FTRs if you like) show an imbalance of orders. when price breaks SR or moves through and engulfs (ignores) S or D. then on first return the excess orders get filled moving the price in that direction, thats all. the visual is this rbd or dbr's that we call FLs or FTRs. all that is, is an imbalance you can exploit on first return, some hold for more than one, and some keep going forming a stack like the one you pointed out. I know it confused me when I was starting out. This is one thing I will look at to see if a Zone is going to work: Following is the Daily. You can see pretty easily that price is trading off a nice level of supply. Just above there is some really nice H4 supply in the blue box. Immediately we know there is nice a potential to FO, and this should be noted in taking any trades around the highs. You can see that price did FO and got into our H4 supply level. This is where we drop down in time frames and look for PA. Following is a H1 chart. One thing I will do when watching PA, is look for an engulf of a flag. If I am at a level on a HTF I won't go too low because it can get a little messy. Now, if this was a TT at H4 supply our stop would have been 90 odd pips, trade taken waiting for conformation on H1 30 odd pips. This is only 1 of many ways looking at PA. Report to moderator Quick Reply Reply Quote Thank You Pedini's trades and setups 01 Jul 2013 23:46 #279 Pedini Topic Author --> Offline Master Trader Posts: 568 Thank you received: 2602 Heya Cas, When drawing Compression PAZ's which is what I drew up on my gold chart, you want to be absolutely sure that price is going to go to the other end of the compression. The only way to do this is to make sure the last pocket of supply or demand has been engulfed. Until this happens, we don't know compression is going to work and really it can go on forever (just look at AUDNZD). Looking at your lines now: 1 - This was a test of a flip level, it formed the drop base rally at 4, but there is still supply above us (so its not the edge of our PAZ) 2 - Again even if this level is broken, which it was, there still remains to be supply above that needs to break. Finally price breaks into our PAZ at 3. This was the last of the supply till the other side of the zone and that is why it is our PAZ level. You can see price then retraced tested out Drop Base Rally at 4 and continued through the zone. I hope this helps, Peds Attachments: Check this box to be notified of replies to this topic. I've seen it written elsewhere on RTM that 'FTR = FL', but you seem to treat it differently, and in a way that chimes with how I've come to think of it. So, it seems to me that the FTR is just confirmation that the FL is current, willing Supply / Demand, but this does not mean that the FTR is current, willing Supply / Demand in and of itself (whether it is or isn't depends on the structure and location of the FTR to my mind). It's this FTR confirmation of the FL which enables us to determine where PAZes are bounded, and where to look for EGs, which show us that current, willing Supply / Demand has now been absorbed, so price will only find more at the next confirmed level out (explaining why price will likely move from one edge of a PAZ to another edge of the adjoining PAZ)... . My conclusion is actually that 'FTR (usually) = FTB' - and thus the FL has already been tested and Supply / Demand removed from it. Perhaps the subtle difference is a matter of how quickly the FL is tested after it is formed? Am I on the right track or wide of the mark? Thanks in advance. Spongy. Report to moderator Quick Reply Reply Quote Thank You Pedini's trades and setups 08 Jul 2013 10:06 #288 Pedini Topic Author --> Offline Master Trader Posts: 568 Thank you received: 2602 Hey guy, just got back from a weekend away, I read your comment on the weekend, but wasn't ready to put my mind from "Break mode" to "Chart mode". Anyway, back into it, YIPEE! Spongy - Going from your comment, and some of your articles you have put together, you really have a talent for tieing information together! As for your question, in my mind this is how I see it (and it may be a simplistic way of viewing it). A FTR is when a level is broken and price fails to get back to higher/lower prices, this failure can be a test of the broken level, or it may fall short, but it is still a FTR. Now, as for your comment regarding a FTR testing and thus removing supply/demand from a flag, again you have this correct IMO, but you may be missing something. I remember when I first started on supply/demand trading I used to watch Sam Seidens webinars. Now Mr Seiden is very strict on teaching not trading a level that is a test of another level (which in our case can be a FTR). To me this is nonsense, just think about how compression forms for example, every time supply/demand is tested in compression it is testing a test of another level, so these levels work! You also have the idea behind the PAZ down well. For me the FTR is more important to engulf and then to look for a trade, rather than basing a trade on the FTR itself (unless it was preceded by an engulf of another FTR). This is all a little bit of a mouthful, I hope it's understood! Hoto - I didn't mark out any CP because there was nothing important to mark off, and as you see the trade was not based on cany CP. You are spot on, those are the exact reasons I marked off those FTR levels Peds Attachments: Check this box to be notified of replies to this topic. Note: BBcode and smileys are still usable. Linked to this is a need to unlearn one 'skill' and add a new one: I need to unlearn trying to pick tops in an uptrend and bottoms in a downtrend (i.e. pay less respect to history, of which this chart was an example); and I need to be more flexible in my approach. The following user(s) said Thank You: faldot Report to moderator Quick Reply Reply Quote Thank You Pedini's trades and setups 31 Jul 2013 00:06 #333 Pedini Topic Author --> Offline Master Trader Posts: 568 Thank you received: 2602 Hey guys, thanks so much for the questions, they are great. At the moment, it is obvious that EU is in a trading range, and there have been some fake moves on either side and trapping people trading the range. I would personally choose to stay out till it resolves itself. As for your questions, what I will do when I see an engulf is ask myself "does this engulf make sense?" By that I mean look at the history around where price engulfed. Did it engulf into a DP or a key level? Did it engulf into supply/demand. Also, look where the source of the engulf came from, was it coming from a HTF supply/demand level or has it failed yet to reach one? All these things should give you a heads up on a potential FO. For example, if price is engulfing south, but price has yet to come off a significant level of supply, it makes sense to see a FO to help push price to higher levels. Something that looks like it may be currently happening on EU. Anyway, I hope this gives some food for thought, it is past 2am, so excuse my lack of a detailed information/charts, I will try to find some example to post when I am well rested. I'll give you some of the opinion I've arrived at (please bear in mind that this is only my view after much thinking: I'm still testing it; it may not align with RTM's view; and it may be inaccurate or plain wrong. Caveat lector (because it's me )). Hiya Pedini, Apologies for jumping on your journal once again! The Engulf matters because it is usually a convincing show of force, but we also have to take into account what it Engulfs, how convincingly it does so, what's beyond it, and what happens directly after. We can Engulf an S / R level, Spike, or Supply / Demand area: to me, that last one matters most as the first two are most likely reactions to it and carry less import (in my eyes, but it depends on the situation). (Hint: you may want to reflect deeply on this paragraph). Here's an update to the chart Pedini and I were discussing in recent posts. The areas marked in grey are what I perceive to be real Supply and Demand: of interest to us right now are the two Supply areas on H4 from way back and the new M30 Demand areas (that bottom chart is actually H1 - I stepped up a time-frame to squeeze all the relevant Price Action in). Warning: Spoiler! [ Click to expand ] [ Click to hide ] As I note in some posts I made recently on the Doctor's journal, I think price has been brought to this area for a reason, so were I trading rather than testing I would actually be stood to one side awaiting the outcome: I expect a great deal of 'directionless volatility' (i.e. whipsawing) this week in 'reaction' to 'major news', many retail traders will be mugged, this will not be by accident. I may be wrong of course, but this looks like a good place and a good time for what I call a honeypot trap, and it's what I would do if I were the Dr. Evil of forex markets. Regards. Spongy. In your UJ example, most of the retraces got rejected at ignored demand (S/R flip) and the trend continued. I've marked these levels on the chart below. You mentioned that these levels are good places to scale in or perhaps take a new trade, however, how would you do this in real time? My dilemma is this - If I take a TT at ignored demand, what if price wants to test the source of the engulf down? That will stop me out. But if I wait for a TT at the source of engulf, I might miss out on most of the move, like in this case. Perhaps a way will be to watch for clues at the ignored demand levels, for example compression towards them. However, compression can last longer than expected, and where does one actually enter and place his stop loss? I guess the safest way would be to watch the LTFs for the classic engulf down followed by a retrace to source of engulf or QM level. Would that be how you look for PA to enter at these ignored demand levels, or do you have some other trick in your book? :) Attachments: Check this box to be notified of replies to this topic. Say you've taken a reversal trade and gotten in at the very bottom, and the trade is hundreds of pips in profit, and you're now managing this trade on the daily TF. I believe that any trade you take subsequent to this on that pair should be taken with absolutely no regard for the original trade. Say your MM has you risk 2% per trade, and your original trade had you buy 1 lot, and you now find yourself with the right PA at the extreme of a very important daily level. You should be able to take this trade according to your normal MM plan, regardless of what other trades you have on the same pair. If it calls for a purchase of 2 lots, then 2 lots is what you should buy, and you should manage this trade completely independently. Certainly it's hard initially to ignore the fact that you're now in for 3 lots on the same pair, but you've got to look at it rationally, leaving fear out of the equation. If this is a currency trade, imagine that the first trade is on something else entirely - imagine you bought a lot of coffee if you must. Remember, our best trades are taken at extremes, and we know the limitations of each trade we take, so we should take every trade on its own merit. Just a thought - have a great weekend :) Check this box to be notified of replies to this topic. Note: BBcode and smileys are still usable. I was also watching USDJPY, with a similar view to go long, but a different rationale. I must admit I did not attach any significance to that pinbar, I just took it as one more clear out of Supply in downwards Compression towards D1 Demand! Now you've highlighted it its importance and the psychology around it make perfect sense - thanks for pointing it out! I posted a few questions in the Classroom (posts #747 to #749 off the top of my head) about trading straight from 'ancient' Supply or Demand areas but nobody took up the challenge of responding (yet?). Hopefully you won't mind me asking some related questions here? Firstly, thinking on your chart, was that pinbar all the confirmation you needed to go long from that D1 Demand? More specifically, the Demand area was from early August so there cannot be unfilled orders from that time still in the market, how can you be sure there will be fresh orders there now, and that there will be enough of them? I was actually waiting on a small area in the shadow of the reaction as you can see in this H4 chart. Warning: Spoiler! [ Click to expand ] [ Click to hide ] Dropping down to M30, what was the significance of the Engulf of that pinbar after you had already entered? Was it just to confirm to you that price would indeed head up now? To me, the pinbar was a reaction to Supply and the Engulf of that pinbar only went deeper into that Supply (i.e. there might still be some left), so was that 'marginal' Engulf enough (it's something I see popping up in other charts as the precursor to a decision to trade)? Warning: Spoiler! [ Click to expand ] [ Click to hide ] This is how I was studying it, hopefully it highlights the importance of the answers to those questions! I have trouble believing in 'ancient' areas of Supply or Demand on longer time-frames. It's not that price doesn't turn at them sometimes , it's just that the orders which cause the reaction to the area are not the remainder of those that created the original area - so if price turns because of new orders, how important is the old area? Too often I've sat waiting for a turn from an 'ancient' area, when none has been forthcoming, and current PA has been telling me something different (and that is not to say my reading of PA is any good ). To me, the importance and definition of areas decays over time until they become either matters of convenience / coincidence, or traps (for S / D traders!). So, with that in mind, I waited to see whether price would react to the area, then looked for something in the shadow of that reaction. Also the Compression into the area might not indicate weakness, so I am not anticipating a turn based on this leading confirmation: as there are fresh areas of Supply, I want to see them taken out first before I'm convinced. In the chart below, I've marked a couple of fresh Supply areas along with the Demand area I was interested in. Ideally I wanted to see proximal Supply get engulfed before the retrace - this didn't happen. There was 'just' the Engulf of your pinbar: would this be enough of a confirmation to take a long from the area I marked, and am I expecting too much waiting on a retrace after Supply (preferably a swing high or low) is broken? Note: on reflection I did actually make a mistake in missing the Supply area responsible for break Support (marked in the chart). The Engulf of this should probably have been enough confirmation to get in (as it happens the Demand area was touched after I had stopped watching charts and started on network certification!). Warning: Spoiler! [ Click to expand ] [ Click to hide ] Note: it's best to start with the bottom three comments to see why I chose the area, then start down from the top to see what I was waiting on :) I spotted the opportunity on M15 so here's that time-frame just in case it helps. Warning: Spoiler! [ Click to expand ] [ Click to hide ] Apologies for making it a long one, seems I can't help myself. Regards. Spongy. So I would have waited to see what happened in the area and based my opportunity off of that, here's some conjecture: Regards. Spongy. Like Pedini said, for us, the H4 supply above was just a level, where we expected price to show us something to trade. So the price came in, made a nice RBD, but this is not enough if it does not engulf the last swing low. If it would have stopped above the last swing low, we would not trade it, since there can still be HHs forming. An engulf of swing low is the PA which says to us, it is relatively safe taking the trade, given somebody who has the might to make an engulf is selling here. Once we have an engulf at a significant level, all we need to do is find a nice place to leave your order and let it do its thing. nothing comes with a guarantee, but sometimes it comes with a high probability! Report to moderator Quick Reply Reply Quote Thank You Pedini's trades and setups 14 Jun 2013 10:58 #203 Pedini Topic Author --> Offline Master Trader Posts: 568 Thank you received: 2602 Hey Hoto. Your points 1, 2 and 3 are all part of the stacked demand. In general when price gets into stacked demand, it normally wants to go through it to the top or bottom level, in this case the bottom level. It is not the same as compression as compression takes out remaining orders while stacked demand still have orders hiding away. But if you think about it logically it will be more profitable to get to the cheapest or most expensive level to trade from... ...you can see from base 1 that price takes off and comes back to re-test the base, these orders have now been filled and it is this point I want to see broken to get into the stacked demand below. This happens as you can see at the circle, and the entry is simply a supply/QM level. You can see now that price returned to the last base in the stacked demand, which is also a flip zone and took off very nicely. I hope this answers both your queries! The following user(s) said Thank You: HotRod , Paichayon , omidfxt , cuimingzhao Report to moderator Quick Reply Reply Quote Thank You Pedini's trades and setups 19 Jun 2013 12:24 #218 HotRod --> Offline Trader Posts: 108 Thank you received: 184 Ahhhh....sweet sweet eureka comes yet again...Thank you! So yes PAZ is any price action or price structure on the chart that shows all opposing levels on the chart have been taken out at some point, and price should cut right through to the last untouched level. Compression is the simplest to understand because the last sentence is all compression is about. But PAZ could take on an infinite number of looks as long as it shows the remaining orders in all opposing levels have been filled. But the PAZ can never include the most recent level because you would not expect price to just cut right through it. So you mark all the violated levels up to the most recent, then when the most recent gets violated it shows that the buyers/sellers are no longer interested in holding price up/down. Thats when you enter on what ever reaction that most recent level caused. Here are 3 charts showing what I got from you. Thank you so much! Actually, does anybody know if it's been explained before? If not, does anybody care to explain it? Sure, it can be found in the PIE thread on FF: Diamonds often occur as an early sign of a reversal and the reason for it is to trap as much retail money as possible, it tends to trap buyers and sellers then resolves very quickly after it completes a cycle of trapping retail. A diamond represents caution above all else because there is no clear defined momentum either way. But from a price structure point of view, its difficult to hold any position, buy or sell for any period of time or profit. Why diamonds occur near reversals is that the market wants to take out all buyers and sellers and then resolve quickly and the shape of the diamond does that. Its a trend traders nightmare and a scalpers or range traders ideal situation. The only way to do this is to make sure the last pocket of supply or demand has been engulfed. Until this happens, we don't know compression is going to work and really it can go on forever (just look at AUDNZD). https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/1184-pedini-s-trades-and-setups?start=275 6/33 7/27/2018 Pedini's trades and setups - Page 12 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT Looking at your lines now: 1 - This was a test of a flip level, it formed the drop base rally at 4, but there is still supply above us (so its not the edge of our PAZ) 2 - Again even if this level is broken, which it was, there still remains to be supply above that needs to break. Finally price breaks into our PAZ at 3. This was the last of the supply till the other side of the zone and that is why it is our PAZ level. You can see price then retraced tested out Drop Base Rally at 4 and continued through the zone. QUICK REPLY REPLY QUOTE THANK YOU Pedini's trades and setups #281 https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/1184-pedini-s-trades-and-setups?start=275 8/33 7/27/2018 Pedini's trades and setups - Page 12 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT Pedini Offline Master Trader Posts: 568 Thank you received: 2620 Hey Cas, Essentially every bar on the charts is part of one PAZ or another. There are all different types. A consolidation in price is a PAZ in itself, it is when this price zone breaks that we get an idea the direction it is going to go, and we can use other price action concepts to enter into a trade. Hopefully this will get a little clearer in the coming weeks. Regarding the chart you posted, it has been something I've been thinking about. I noticed that in a strong trend, very often price doesn't retrace to the source of engulf for us to take a conventional TT entry. In your UJ example, most of the retraces got rejected at ignored demand (S/R flip) and the trend continued. I've marked these levels on the chart below. You mentioned that these levels are good places to scale in or perhaps take a new trade, however, how would you do this in real time? My dilemma is this - If I take a TT at ignored demand, what if price wants to test the source of the engulf down? That will stop me out. But if I wait for a TT at the source of engulf, I might miss out on most of the move, like in this case. Perhaps a way will be to watch for clues at the ignored demand levels, for example compression towards them. Say you've taken a reversal trade and gotten in at the very bottom, and the trade is hundreds of pips in profit, and you're now managing this trade on the daily TF. I believe that any trade you take subsequent to this on that pair should be taken with absolutely no regard for the original trade. Say your MM has you risk 2% per trade, and your original trade had you buy 1 lot, and you now find yourself with the right PA at the extreme of a very important daily level. You should be able to take this trade according to your normal MM plan, regardless of what other trades you have on the same pair. If it calls for a purchase of 2 lots, then 2 https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/1184-pedini-s-trades-and-setups?start=350 28/33 7/27/2018 Pedini's trades and setups - Page 15 - RTM Community lots is what you should buy, and you should manage this trade completely HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT independently. Certainly it's hard initially to ignore the fact that you're now in for 3 lots on the same pair, but you've got to look at it rationally, leaving fear out of the equation. If this is a currency trade, imagine that the first trade is on something else entirely - imagine you bought a lot of coffee if you must. Remember, our best trades are taken at extremes, and we know the limitations of each trade we take, so we should take every trade on its own merit. What is that 1,2,3 you have marked tells us. Regards Fxyogi Hiya man, no trouble at all! 1. This is a really good question, and yes the supply level you marked is clean supply. There are however plenty of supply/demand traders waiting there to short as well. If I had a bucket load of money to put into the market, and I knew where the majority of the crowd want to short I can push price higher, take their stops, and turn price at the last possible chance. Was I granted to get my fill, no. But I knew it was the safest short I could take. 2. The 1, 2, 3 is the "three drive pattern" (there is an article about it in Markepedia). The important thing here is how price has an explosive move up, then tests demand before moving up again. Demand is being consumed on the way up, for an easy return journey. [ Click to expand ] Dropping down to M30, what was the significance of the Engulf of that pinbar after you had already entered? Was it just to confirm to you that price would indeed head up now? To me, the pinbar was a reaction to Supply and the Engulf of that pinbar only went deeper into that Supply (i.e. there might still be some left), so was that 'marginal' Engulf enough (it's something I see popping up in other charts as the precursor to a decision to trade)? Warning: Spoiler! [ Click to expand ] This is how I was studying it, hopefully it highlights the importance of the answers to those questions! I have trouble believing in 'ancient' areas of Supply or Demand on longer time-frames. It's not that price doesn't turn at them sometimes, it's just that the orders which cause https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/1184-pedini-s-trades-and-setups?start=425 4/40 7/27/2018 Pedini's trades and setups - Page 18 - RTM Community the reaction to the area are not the remainder of those that created the original area - HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT so if price turns because of new orders, how important is the old area? Too often I've sat waiting for a turn from an 'ancient' area, when none has been forthcoming, and current PA has been telling me something different (and that is not to say my reading of PA is any good ). To me, the importance and definition of areas decays over time until they become either matters of convenience / coincidence, or traps (for S / D traders!). So, with that in mind, I waited to see whether price would react to the area, then looked for something in the shadow of that reaction. Also the Compression into the area might not indicate weakness, so I am not anticipating a turn based on this leading confirmation: as there are fresh areas of Supply, I want to see them taken out first before I'm convinced. In the chart below, I've marked a couple of fresh Supply areas along with the Demand area I was interested in. Ideally I wanted to see proximal Supply get engulfed before the retrace - this didn't happen. There was 'just' the Engulf of your pinbar: would this be enough of a confirmation to take a long from the area I marked, and am I expecting too much waiting on a retrace after Supply (preferably a swing high or low) is broken? Note: on reflection I did actually make a mistake in missing the Supply area responsible for break Support (marked in the chart). The Engulf of this should probably have been enough confirmation to get in (as it happens the Demand area was touched after I had stopped watching charts and started on network certification!). Like Pedini said, for us, the H4 supply above was just a level, where we expected price to show us something to trade. So the price came in, made a nice RBD, but this is not enough if it does not engulf the last swing low. If it would have stopped above the last swing low, we would not trade it, since there can still be HHs forming. An engulf of swing low is the PA which says to us, it is relatively safe taking the trade, given somebody who has the might to make an engulf is selling here. Once we have an engulf at a significant level, all we need to do is find a nice place to leave your order and let it do its thing. nothing comes with a guarantee, but sometimes it comes with a high probability! QUICK REPLY REPLY QUOTE THANK YOU Pedini's trades and setups #203 Pedini Offline Master Trader Posts: 568 Thank you received: 2620 Hey Hoto. Your points 1, 2 and 3 are all part of the stacked demand. In general when price gets into stacked demand, it normally wants to go through it to the top or bottom level, in this case the bottom level. It is not the same as compression as compression takes out remaining orders while stacked demand still have orders hiding away. But if you think about it logically it will be more profitable to get to the cheapest or most expensive level to trade from... ...you can see from base 1 that price takes off and comes back to re-test the base, these orders have now been filled and it is this point I want to see broken to get into the stacked demand below. This happens as you can see at the circle, and the entry is simply a supply/QM level. You can see now that price returned to the last base in the stacked demand, which is also a flip zone and took off very nicely. https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/1184-pedini-s-trades-and-setups?start=200 4/35 7/27/2018 Pedini's trades and setups - Page 9 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT I hope this answers both your queries! Peds Attachments: The following user(s) said Thank You: HotRod, Paichayon, omidfxt, cuimingzhao QUICK REPLY REPLY QUOTE THANK YOU Pedini's trades and setups #218 https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/1184-pedini-s-trades-and-setups?start=200 23/35 7/27/2018 Pedini's trades and setups - Page 9 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT HotRod Offline Trader Posts: 108 Thank you received: 189 Ahhhh....sweet sweet eureka comes yet again...Thank you! So yes PAZ is any price action or price structure on the chart that shows all opposing levels on the chart have been taken out at some point, and price should cut right through to the last untouched level. Compression is the simplest to understand because the last sentence is all compression is about. But PAZ could take on an infinite number of looks as long as it shows the remaining orders in all opposing levels have been filled. But the PAZ can never include the most recent level because you would not expect price to just cut right through it. So you mark all the violated levels up to the most recent, then when the most recent gets violated it shows that the buyers/sellers are no longer interested in holding price up/down. Thats when you enter on what ever reaction that most recent level caused. Here are 3 charts showing what I got from you. The following user(s) said Thank You: Steigo , cuimingzhao With time, patience and experience, what once seemed very complex becomes very simple indeed Please join www.theblue.community Report to moderator Quick Reply Reply Quote Thank You Pedini's trades and setups 20 Aug 2012 03:10 #6 homerus --> Offline Trader Posts: 115 Thank you received: 112 Ifmyante wrote: Have you read anything by Red about the diamond? Actually, does anybody know if it's been explained before? If not, does anybody care to explain it? Sure, it can be found in the PIE thread on FF: Diamonds often occur as an early sign of a reversal and the reason for it is to trap as much retail money as possible, it tends to trap buyers and sellers then resolves very quickly after it completes a cycle of trapping retail. A diamond represents caution above all else because there is no clear defined momentum either way. But from a price structure point of view, its difficult to hold any position, buy or sell for any period of time or profit. Why diamonds occur near reversals is that the market wants to take out all buyers and sellers and then resolve quickly and the shape of the diamond does that. Its a trend traders nightmare and a scalpers or range traders ideal situation. Check this box to be notified of replies to this topic. Note: BBcode and smileys are still usable. Report to moderator Quick Reply Reply Quote Thank You Pedini's trades and setups 23 Jun 2013 05:31 #241 Harry --> Offline Master Trader Posts: 941 Thank you received: 2903 Hotochin wrote: Hey Harry I have got a question for you. How do you know that is the FL? Sometimes you will get multiple RBR levels that could act as FL. Even in your chart, couldn't that level below make a FL? Thanks, H you are quite right there Hotochin, you see FLs (or FTRs if you like) show an imbalance of orders. when price breaks SR or moves through and engulfs (ignores) S or D. then on first return the excess orders get filled moving the price in that direction, thats all. the visual is this rbd or dbr's that we call FLs or FTRs. all that is, is an imbalance you can exploit on first return, some hold for more than one, and some keep going forming a stack like the one you pointed out. Report to moderator Quick Reply Reply Quote Thank You Pedini's trades and setups 01 Jul 2013 23:46 #279 Pedini Topic Author --> Offline Master Trader Posts: 568 Thank you received: 2602 Heya Cas, When drawing Compression PAZ's which is what I drew up on my gold chart, you want to be absolutely sure that price is going to go to the other end of the compression. The only way to do this is to make sure the last pocket of supply or demand has been engulfed. Until this happens, we don't know compression is going to work and really it can go on forever (just look at AUDNZD). Looking at your lines now: 1 - This was a test of a flip level, it formed the drop base rally at 4, but there is still supply above us (so its not the edge of our PAZ) 2 - Again even if this level is broken, which it was, there still remains to be supply above that needs to break. Finally price breaks into our PAZ at 3. This was the last of the supply till the other side of the zone and that is why it is our PAZ level. You can see price then retraced tested out Drop Base Rally at 4 and continued through the zone. I hope this helps, Peds Attachments: Check this box to be notified of replies to this topic. I've seen it written elsewhere on RTM that 'FTR = FL', but you seem to treat it differently, and in a way that chimes with how I've come to think of it. So, it seems to me that the FTR is just confirmation that the FL is current, willing Supply / Demand, but this does not mean that the FTR is current, willing Supply / Demand in and of itself (whether it is or isn't depends on the structure and location of the FTR to my mind). It's this FTR confirmation of the FL which enables us to determine where PAZes are bounded, and where to look for EGs, which show us that current, willing Supply / Demand has now been absorbed, so price will only find more at the next confirmed level out (explaining why price will likely move from one edge of a PAZ to another edge of the adjoining PAZ)... . My conclusion is actually that 'FTR (usually) = FTB' - and thus the FL has already been tested and Supply / Demand removed from it. Perhaps the subtle difference is a matter of how quickly the FL is tested after it is formed? Am I on the right track or wide of the mark? Thanks in advance. Spongy. Anyway, back into it, YIPEE! Spongy - Going from your comment, and some of your articles you have put together, you really have a talent for tieing information together! As for your question, in my mind this is how I see it (and it may be a simplistic way of viewing it). A FTR is when a level is broken and price fails to get back to higher/lower prices, this failure can be a test of the broken level, or it may fall short, but it is still a FTR. Now, as for your comment regarding a FTR testing and thus removing supply/demand from a flag, again you have this correct IMO, but you may be missing something. I remember when I first started on supply/demand trading I used to watch Sam Seidens webinars. Now Mr Seiden is very strict on teaching not trading a level that is a test of another level (which in our case can be a FTR). To me this is nonsense, just think about how compression forms for example, every time supply/demand is tested in compression it is testing a test of another level, so these levels work! You also have the idea behind the PAZ down well. For me the FTR is more important to engulf and then to look for a trade, rather than basing a trade on the FTR itself (unless it was preceded by an engulf of another FTR). This is all a little bit of a mouthful, I hope it's understood! Hoto - I didn't mark out any CP because there was nothing important to mark off, and as you see the trade was not based on cany CP. You are spot on, those are the exact reasons I marked off those FTR levels Peds Attachments: Check this box to be notified of replies to this topic. Note: BBcode and smileys are still usable. Current Price Action tells us what's going to happen next, and if it coincides with old stuff, perhaps that's a nice secondary factor in making a decision. Now all I need to do is read current Price Action successfully! So, I was actually more interested in seeing whether that M30 Demand would hold, regardless of the H4 Supply from yesteryear, and as it did I'm not surprised at the Engulf of both those prospective M30 Supply levels I'd marked (in fact after I'd posted it I'd wished I'd continued my red line upwards past those levels for a Fake Out, c'est la vie). Warning: Spoiler! [ Click to expand ] [ Click to hide ] What happens next will be of interest though as price has potentially Engulfed that H4 Supply in the process (by 0.2 pip according to my data provider - but to me that's random variation to be ignored). Will price Break Out or Fake Out now? If it's a Fake Out it needs to Engulf that M30 Demand I marked (which means the new Demand above it, and preferably the unmarked one just below it) to convince me, if it's a Break Out, then it's a potential drag race to D1 Supply (not shown on these charts, but there is nothing in the way of price until it gets there). Still, at the moment I'm just drawing areas and practicing after spending a lot of recent time pondering exactly what an Engulf means and the importance of what happens after it. Hopefully I'll have something to show for the effort and my new understanding (or I'll trip at the hurdle and have to go through the loop again ). Linked to this is a need to unlearn one 'skill' and add a new one: I need to unlearn trying to pick tops in an uptrend and bottoms in a downtrend (i.e. pay less respect to history, of which this chart was an example); and I need to be more flexible in my approach. I think the key to achieving both is how I think of Engulfs now. The proof is very much in the pudding at the moment, so I hope it's a giant, brandy-soaked Christmas Pudding with a litre of double cream and not some sugar-free, fat-free, flavour-free offence to all right-thinking people. Ooh, and as I've been writing this, price has stabbed down: how far will it get? Regards. Spongy. Check this box to be notified of replies to this topic. Note: BBcode and smileys are still usable. The following user(s) said Thank You: faldot Report to moderator Quick Reply Reply Quote Thank You Pedini's trades and setups 31 Jul 2013 00:06 #333 Pedini Topic Author --> Offline Master Trader Posts: 568 Thank you received: 2602 Hey guys, thanks so much for the questions, they are great. At the moment, it is obvious that EU is in a trading range, and there have been some fake moves on either side and trapping people trading the range. I would personally choose to stay out till it resolves itself. As for your questions, what I will do when I see an engulf is ask myself "does this engulf make sense?" By that I mean look at the history around where price engulfed. Did it engulf into a DP or a key level? Did it engulf into supply/demand. Also, look where the source of the engulf came from, was it coming from a HTF supply/demand level or has it failed yet to reach one? All these things should give you a heads up on a potential FO. For example, if price is engulfing south, but price has yet to come off a significant level of supply, it makes sense to see a FO to help push price to higher levels. Something that looks like it may be currently happening on EU. Anyway, I hope this gives some food for thought, it is past 2am, so excuse my lack of a detailed information/charts, I will try to find some example to post when I am well rested. I'll give you some of the opinion I've arrived at (please bear in mind that this is only my view after much thinking: I'm still testing it; it may not align with RTM's view; and it may be inaccurate or plain wrong. Caveat lector (because it's me )). Hiya Pedini, Apologies for jumping on your journal once again! The Engulf matters because it is usually a convincing show of force, but we also have to take into account what it Engulfs, how convincingly it does so, what's beyond it, and what happens directly after. We can Engulf an S / R level, Spike, or Supply / Demand area: to me, that last one matters most as the first two are most likely reactions to it and carry less import (in my eyes, but it depends on the situation). (Hint: you may want to reflect deeply on this paragraph). Here's an update to the chart Pedini and I were discussing in recent posts. The areas marked in grey are what I perceive to be real Supply and Demand: of interest to us right now are the two Supply areas on H4 from way back and the new M30 Demand areas (that bottom chart is actually H1 - I stepped up a time-frame to squeeze all the relevant Price Action in). Warning: Spoiler! [ Click to expand ] [ Click to hide ] As I note in some posts I made recently on the Doctor's journal, I think price has been brought to this area for a reason, so were I trading rather than testing I would actually be stood to one side awaiting the outcome: I expect a great deal of 'directionless volatility' (i.e. whipsawing) this week in 'reaction' to 'major news', many retail traders will be mugged, this will not be by accident. I may be wrong of course, but this looks like a good place and a good time for what I call a honeypot trap, and it's what I would do if I were the Dr. Evil of forex markets. Regards. Spongy. Regarding the chart you posted, it has been something I've been thinking about. I noticed that in a strong trend, very often price doesn't retrace to the source of engulf for us to take a conventional TT entry. In your UJ example, most of the retraces got rejected at ignored demand (S/R flip) and the trend continued. I've marked these levels on the chart below. You mentioned that these levels are good places to scale in or perhaps take a new trade, however, how would you do this in real time? My dilemma is this - If I take a TT at ignored demand, what if price wants to test the source of the engulf down? That will stop me out. But if I wait for a TT at the source of engulf, I might miss out on most of the move, like in this case. Perhaps a way will be to watch for clues at the ignored demand levels, for example compression towards them. However, compression can last longer than expected, and where does one actually enter and place his stop loss? I guess the safest way would be to watch the LTFs for the classic engulf down followed by a retrace to source of engulf or QM level. Would that be how you look for PA to enter at these ignored demand levels, or do you have some other trick in your book? :) Attachments: Check this box to be notified of replies to this topic. The following user(s) said Thank You: cuimingzhao Whatever the mind can conceive and believe, it can achieve - Napolean Hill Report to moderator Quick Reply Reply Quote Thank You Pedini's trades and setups 10 Aug 2013 18:59 #372 Ifmyante --> Offline Chief Cook and Bottle Washer If you see a piece of truth glistening in the dirt, get down on your knees and gently dig it out, for it's the greatest treasure you will ever find Posts: 3574 Thank you received: 14393 Sorry for butting into your journal here Pedini, but I'm itching to comment on this discussion. Say you've taken a reversal trade and gotten in at the very bottom, and the trade is hundreds of pips in profit, and you're now managing this trade on the daily TF. I believe that any trade you take subsequent to this on that pair should be taken with absolutely no regard for the original trade. Say your MM has you risk 2% per trade, and your original trade had you buy 1 lot, and you now find yourself with the right PA at the extreme of a very important daily level. You should be able to take this trade according to your normal MM plan, regardless of what other trades you have on the same pair. If it calls for a purchase of 2 lots, then 2 lots is what you should buy, and you should manage this trade completely independently. Certainly it's hard initially to ignore the fact that you're now in for 3 lots on the same pair, but you've got to look at it rationally, leaving fear out of the equation. If this is a currency trade, imagine that the first trade is on something else entirely - imagine you bought a lot of coffee if you must. Remember, our best trades are taken at extremes, and we know the limitations of each trade we take, so we should take every trade on its own merit. Just a thought - have a great weekend :) Check this box to be notified of replies to this topic. Note: BBcode and smileys are still usable. Peds Hi Pedini , I am new to this forum but not new to supply demand trading. You guys are doing amazing job. So far unlike other forums , i never found traders scolding other traders for not understanding the teachings. there are no "Read between the lines", "We don't spoon feed baby's here". Getting back to this chart you attached, I am really thinking how you define FTR, the term is confusing for many of us. why we say it as failure to return?. to what it fails to return?. Hopefully you won't mind me asking some related questions here? Firstly, thinking on your chart, was that pinbar all the confirmation you needed to go long from that D1 Demand? More specifically, the Demand area was from early August so there cannot be unfilled orders from that time still in the market, how can you be sure there will be fresh orders there now, and that there will be enough of them? I was actually waiting on a small area in the shadow of the reaction as you can see in this H4 chart. Warning: Spoiler! [ Click to expand ] [ Click to hide ] Dropping down to M30, what was the significance of the Engulf of that pinbar after you had already entered? Was it just to confirm to you that price would indeed head up now? To me, the pinbar was a reaction to Supply and the Engulf of that pinbar only went deeper into that Supply (i.e. there might still be some left), so was that 'marginal' Engulf enough (it's something I see popping up in other charts as the precursor to a decision to trade)? Warning: Spoiler! [ Click to expand ] [ Click to hide ] This is how I was studying it, hopefully it highlights the importance of the answers to those questions! I have trouble believing in 'ancient' areas of Supply or Demand on longer time-frames. It's not that price doesn't turn at them sometimes , it's just that the orders which cause the reaction to the area are not the remainder of those that created the original area - so if price turns because of new orders, how important is the old area? Too often I've sat waiting for a turn from an 'ancient' area, when none has been forthcoming, and current PA has been telling me something different (and that is not to say my reading of PA is any good ). To me, the importance and definition of areas decays over time until they become either matters of convenience / coincidence, or traps (for S / D traders!). So, with that in mind, I waited to see whether price would react to the area, then looked for something in the shadow of that reaction. Also the Compression into the area might not indicate weakness, so I am not anticipating a turn based on this leading confirmation: as there are fresh areas of Supply, I want to see them taken out first before I'm convinced. In the chart below, I've marked a couple of fresh Supply areas along with the Demand area I was interested in. Ideally I wanted to see proximal Supply get engulfed before the retrace - this didn't happen. There was 'just' the Engulf of your pinbar: would this be enough of a confirmation to take a long from the area I marked, and am I expecting too much waiting on a retrace after Supply (preferably a swing high or low) is broken? Note: on reflection I did actually make a mistake in missing the Supply area responsible for break Support (marked in the chart). The Engulf of this should probably have been enough confirmation to get in (as it happens the Demand area was touched after I had stopped watching charts and started on network certification!). Warning: Spoiler! Warning: Spoiler! [ Click to expand ] [ Click to hide ] Apologies for making it a long one, seems I can't help myself. Regards. Spongy. [ Click to expand ] [ Click to hide ] W1 - the nature of that reaction to potential Demand, confirms it as a strong source of buyer interest - Pro Money. The level is placed at the bottom of that reaction as there are confirmed orders around here. There's still buying interest when price returns much later, but it's not Pro Money interest - it's just the liquidity for Pro Money to drive price down: D1 - a close up on the break below that level. There's an EG or FO of it, but we don't know which until we see what happens next. There isn't a new high after, so it's not FO. A further EG takes out Demand, then price is driven down hard - FTR. I don't have H4 history, but I would be happy enough picking that one green candle as the basis of new Supply (note: I might just have easily selected only the top wick and ignored the body. I included the body this time because it shows the point where late buyers were crushed). Also, my view (is this shared?) of FTRs is that they can be a source of Supply or Demand, or they just confirm its presence by being reactions to it, so clipping the top of the FTR but placing the Stop above highs or lows to its left covers both horses, so to speak: H4 - because of the the way I marked Supply on D1, I actually see an Entry, it could easily have been otherwise - it still misses the level marked for the bottom of that reaction seen way back on W1. I've marked what seem like reasonable TPs, but my view (for now) is that price is hasn't finished going up yet, so I don't think TP2 is likely: H4 - and just to be awkward (who me? ) I wouldn't actually have taken the trade as marked for two reasons/beliefs: that price information integrity decays over time because of anticipation and interpretation, so that the way price is moved at these areas is very much a matter of convenience based on where current liquidity is, or where it can be induced, or which direction it's pointing in; and that accuracy is not so important anyway, where there are such differences in price feeds between brokers (a trader's hit on one platform is a miss on another, candles and levels can vary so the candles and formations I see may not be the ones anyone else sees... .). So I would have waited to see what happened in the area and based my opportunity off of that, here's some conjecture: Regards. Spongy. Do you just depend on original DBR and RBD for macro trend REVERSAL spots?? Your level circled in green will most likely hold some importance in a lower timeframe, it doesn't look to amazing to me there though, however it still has the potential to bounce price. Again, it depends how price approaches it etc. Peds Check this box to be notified of replies to this topic. Note: BBcode and smileys are still usable. The following user(s) said Thank You: alirezat Report to moderator Quick Reply Reply Quote Thank You Pedini's trades and setups 28 Apr 2013 17:01 #139 sunnytrader1984 --> Offline Associate Trader Posts: 375 Thank you received: 731 @Infest as you said there are several ways to trade this setup and I in no ways would argue to that, everybody who trades, trades in his own way. Like Pedini said, for us, the H4 supply above was just a level, where we expected price to show us something to trade. So the price came in, made a nice RBD, but this is not enough if it does not engulf the last swing low. If it would have stopped above the last swing low, we would not trade it, since there can still be HHs forming. An engulf of swing low is the PA which says to us, it is relatively safe taking the trade, given somebody who has the might to make an engulf is selling here. Once we have an engulf at a significant level, all we need to do is find a nice place to leave your order and let it do its thing. nothing comes with a guarantee, but sometimes it comes with a high probability! Report to moderator Quick Reply Reply Quote Thank You Pedini's trades and setups 14 Jun 2013 10:58 #203 Pedini Topic Author --> Offline Master Trader Posts: 568 Thank you received: 2602 Hey Hoto. Your points 1, 2 and 3 are all part of the stacked demand. In general when price gets into stacked demand, it normally wants to go through it to the top or bottom level, in this case the bottom level. It is not the same as compression as compression takes out remaining orders while stacked demand still have orders hiding away. But if you think about it logically it will be more profitable to get to the cheapest or most expensive level to trade from... ...you can see from base 1 that price takes off and comes back to re-test the base, these orders have now been filled and it is this point I want to see broken to get into the stacked demand below. This happens as you can see at the circle, and the entry is simply a supply/QM level. You can see now that price returned to the last base in the stacked demand, which is also a flip zone and took off very nicely. I hope this answers both your queries! The following user(s) said Thank You: HotRod , Paichayon , omidfxt , cuimingzhao Report to moderator Quick Reply Reply Quote Thank You Pedini's trades and setups 19 Jun 2013 12:24 #218 HotRod --> Offline Trader Posts: 108 Thank you received: 184 Ahhhh....sweet sweet eureka comes yet again...Thank you! So yes PAZ is any price action or price structure on the chart that shows all opposing levels on the chart have been taken out at some point, and price should cut right through to the last untouched level. Compression is the simplest to understand because the last sentence is all compression is about. But PAZ could take on an infinite number of looks as long as it shows the remaining orders in all opposing levels have been filled. But the PAZ can never include the most recent level because you would not expect price to just cut right through it. So you mark all the violated levels up to the most recent, then when the most recent gets violated it shows that the buyers/sellers are no longer interested in holding price up/down. Thats when you enter on what ever reaction that most recent level caused. Here are 3 charts showing what I got from you. Thank you so much! Actually, does anybody know if it's been explained before? If not, does anybody care to explain it? Sure, it can be found in the PIE thread on FF: Diamonds often occur as an early sign of a reversal and the reason for it is to trap as much retail money as possible, it tends to trap buyers and sellers then resolves very quickly after it completes a cycle of trapping retail. A diamond represents caution above all else because there is no clear defined momentum either way. But from a price structure point of view, its difficult to hold any position, buy or sell for any period of time or profit. Why diamonds occur near reversals is that the market wants to take out all buyers and sellers and then resolve quickly and the shape of the diamond does that. Its a trend traders nightmare and a scalpers or range traders ideal situation. The only way to do this is to make sure the last pocket of supply or demand has been engulfed. Until this happens, we don't know compression is going to work and really it can go on forever (just look at AUDNZD). https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/1184-pedini-s-trades-and-setups?start=275 6/33 7/27/2018 Pedini's trades and setups - Page 12 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT Looking at your lines now: 1 - This was a test of a flip level, it formed the drop base rally at 4, but there is still supply above us (so its not the edge of our PAZ) 2 - Again even if this level is broken, which it was, there still remains to be supply above that needs to break. Finally price breaks into our PAZ at 3. This was the last of the supply till the other side of the zone and that is why it is our PAZ level. You can see price then retraced tested out Drop Base Rally at 4 and continued through the zone. QUICK REPLY REPLY QUOTE THANK YOU Pedini's trades and setups #281 https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/1184-pedini-s-trades-and-setups?start=275 8/33 7/27/2018 Pedini's trades and setups - Page 12 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT Pedini Offline Master Trader Posts: 568 Thank you received: 2620 Hey Cas, Essentially every bar on the charts is part of one PAZ or another. There are all different types. A consolidation in price is a PAZ in itself, it is when this price zone breaks that we get an idea the direction it is going to go, and we can use other price action concepts to enter into a trade. Hopefully this will get a little clearer in the coming weeks. Regarding the chart you posted, it has been something I've been thinking about. I noticed that in a strong trend, very often price doesn't retrace to the source of engulf for us to take a conventional TT entry. In your UJ example, most of the retraces got rejected at ignored demand (S/R flip) and the trend continued. I've marked these levels on the chart below. You mentioned that these levels are good places to scale in or perhaps take a new trade, however, how would you do this in real time? My dilemma is this - If I take a TT at ignored demand, what if price wants to test the source of the engulf down? That will stop me out. But if I wait for a TT at the source of engulf, I might miss out on most of the move, like in this case. Perhaps a way will be to watch for clues at the ignored demand levels, for example compression towards them. Say you've taken a reversal trade and gotten in at the very bottom, and the trade is hundreds of pips in profit, and you're now managing this trade on the daily TF. I believe that any trade you take subsequent to this on that pair should be taken with absolutely no regard for the original trade. Say your MM has you risk 2% per trade, and your original trade had you buy 1 lot, and you now find yourself with the right PA at the extreme of a very important daily level. You should be able to take this trade according to your normal MM plan, regardless of what other trades you have on the same pair. If it calls for a purchase of 2 lots, then 2 https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/1184-pedini-s-trades-and-setups?start=350 28/33 7/27/2018 Pedini's trades and setups - Page 15 - RTM Community lots is what you should buy, and you should manage this trade completely HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT independently. Certainly it's hard initially to ignore the fact that you're now in for 3 lots on the same pair, but you've got to look at it rationally, leaving fear out of the equation. If this is a currency trade, imagine that the first trade is on something else entirely - imagine you bought a lot of coffee if you must. Remember, our best trades are taken at extremes, and we know the limitations of each trade we take, so we should take every trade on its own merit. What is that 1,2,3 you have marked tells us. Regards Fxyogi Hiya man, no trouble at all! 1. This is a really good question, and yes the supply level you marked is clean supply. There are however plenty of supply/demand traders waiting there to short as well. If I had a bucket load of money to put into the market, and I knew where the majority of the crowd want to short I can push price higher, take their stops, and turn price at the last possible chance. Was I granted to get my fill, no. But I knew it was the safest short I could take. 2. The 1, 2, 3 is the "three drive pattern" (there is an article about it in Markepedia). The important thing here is how price has an explosive move up, then tests demand before moving up again. Demand is being consumed on the way up, for an easy return journey. [ Click to expand ] Dropping down to M30, what was the significance of the Engulf of that pinbar after you had already entered? Was it just to confirm to you that price would indeed head up now? To me, the pinbar was a reaction to Supply and the Engulf of that pinbar only went deeper into that Supply (i.e. there might still be some left), so was that 'marginal' Engulf enough (it's something I see popping up in other charts as the precursor to a decision to trade)? Warning: Spoiler! [ Click to expand ] This is how I was studying it, hopefully it highlights the importance of the answers to those questions! I have trouble believing in 'ancient' areas of Supply or Demand on longer time-frames. It's not that price doesn't turn at them sometimes, it's just that the orders which cause https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/1184-pedini-s-trades-and-setups?start=425 4/40 7/27/2018 Pedini's trades and setups - Page 18 - RTM Community the reaction to the area are not the remainder of those that created the original area - HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT so if price turns because of new orders, how important is the old area? Too often I've sat waiting for a turn from an 'ancient' area, when none has been forthcoming, and current PA has been telling me something different (and that is not to say my reading of PA is any good ). To me, the importance and definition of areas decays over time until they become either matters of convenience / coincidence, or traps (for S / D traders!). So, with that in mind, I waited to see whether price would react to the area, then looked for something in the shadow of that reaction. Also the Compression into the area might not indicate weakness, so I am not anticipating a turn based on this leading confirmation: as there are fresh areas of Supply, I want to see them taken out first before I'm convinced. In the chart below, I've marked a couple of fresh Supply areas along with the Demand area I was interested in. Ideally I wanted to see proximal Supply get engulfed before the retrace - this didn't happen. There was 'just' the Engulf of your pinbar: would this be enough of a confirmation to take a long from the area I marked, and am I expecting too much waiting on a retrace after Supply (preferably a swing high or low) is broken? Note: on reflection I did actually make a mistake in missing the Supply area responsible for break Support (marked in the chart). The Engulf of this should probably have been enough confirmation to get in (as it happens the Demand area was touched after I had stopped watching charts and started on network certification!). Like Pedini said, for us, the H4 supply above was just a level, where we expected price to show us something to trade. So the price came in, made a nice RBD, but this is not enough if it does not engulf the last swing low. If it would have stopped above the last swing low, we would not trade it, since there can still be HHs forming. An engulf of swing low is the PA which says to us, it is relatively safe taking the trade, given somebody who has the might to make an engulf is selling here. Once we have an engulf at a significant level, all we need to do is find a nice place to leave your order and let it do its thing. nothing comes with a guarantee, but sometimes it comes with a high probability! QUICK REPLY REPLY QUOTE THANK YOU Pedini's trades and setups #203 Pedini Offline Master Trader Posts: 568 Thank you received: 2620 Hey Hoto. Your points 1, 2 and 3 are all part of the stacked demand. In general when price gets into stacked demand, it normally wants to go through it to the top or bottom level, in this case the bottom level. It is not the same as compression as compression takes out remaining orders while stacked demand still have orders hiding away. But if you think about it logically it will be more profitable to get to the cheapest or most expensive level to trade from... ...you can see from base 1 that price takes off and comes back to re-test the base, these orders have now been filled and it is this point I want to see broken to get into the stacked demand below. This happens as you can see at the circle, and the entry is simply a supply/QM level. You can see now that price returned to the last base in the stacked demand, which is also a flip zone and took off very nicely. https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/1184-pedini-s-trades-and-setups?start=200 4/35 7/27/2018 Pedini's trades and setups - Page 9 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT I hope this answers both your queries! Peds Attachments: The following user(s) said Thank You: HotRod, Paichayon, omidfxt, cuimingzhao QUICK REPLY REPLY QUOTE THANK YOU Pedini's trades and setups #218 https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/1184-pedini-s-trades-and-setups?start=200 23/35 7/27/2018 Pedini's trades and setups - Page 9 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT HotRod Offline Trader Posts: 108 Thank you received: 189 Ahhhh....sweet sweet eureka comes yet again...Thank you! So yes PAZ is any price action or price structure on the chart that shows all opposing levels on the chart have been taken out at some point, and price should cut right through to the last untouched level. Compression is the simplest to understand because the last sentence is all compression is about. But PAZ could take on an infinite number of looks as long as it shows the remaining orders in all opposing levels have been filled. But the PAZ can never include the most recent level because you would not expect price to just cut right through it. So you mark all the violated levels up to the most recent, then when the most recent gets violated it shows that the buyers/sellers are no longer interested in holding price up/down. Thats when you enter on what ever reaction that most recent level caused. Here are 3 charts showing what I got from you.
